title: Statement Levels Explained: Requirement, Recommendation, Permission

body.abstract:
This profile is a teaching example. It shows how a single YAML configuration drives three distinct kinds of statement — a *requirement* (SHALL), a *recommendation* (SHOULD) and a *permission* (MAY) — and how the profile builder renders each one differently and treats only requirements as conformance-tested.

Each statement below is labelled by the builder according to one field, `level`. That single field determines the Metanorma block type, the identifier namespace (`/req/`, `/rec/` or `/per/`), the generated filename (`REQ_`, `REC_` or `PER_`) and — most importantly — whether the statement is checked by the Abstract Test Suite in Annex A.

clauses.title: How to read this document
clauses.body:
The three statements that follow are identical in every respect except their *level*. Read them together to see what the level controls.

=== Requirement (SHALL)

A requirement is normative. It is the only statement level that is conformance-tested: every requirement has a matching abstract test in Annex A, and an implementation that does not meet it is non-conformant. Requirements are rendered as a *Requirement* box and carry a `/req/` identifier.

=== Recommendation (SHOULD)

A recommendation is informative best practice. It is published as guidance but is *not* conformance-tested — an implementation that does not follow it is still conformant. Recommendations are rendered as a *Recommendation* box and carry a `/rec/` identifier. They never appear in the Abstract Test Suite.

=== Permission (MAY)

A permission is an explicitly allowed option. Like a recommendation it is informative and not conformance-tested. Permissions are rendered as a *Permission* box and carry a `/per/` identifier.

=== What this means for conformance

Of the three statements below, only the requirement is listed in the Annex A Abstract Test Suite. The recommendation and permission are reported in the profile's quality summary as informative, but they can never make an implementation non-conformant. The author expresses all of this with one field — `level` — and the tooling does the rest.

requirement_intros.req/output-geojson: This statement uses SHALL, so the builder renders it as a Requirement box with a /req/ identifier and generates a matching abstract test in Annex A. It is conformance-tested.
requirement_intros.rec/document-units: This statement uses SHOULD, so the builder renders it as a Recommendation box with a /rec/ identifier. It is published as guidance and is NOT conformance-tested — note that it has no entry in Annex A.
requirement_intros.per/support-post: This statement uses MAY, so the builder renders it as a Permission box with a /per/ identifier. It describes an allowed option and is NOT conformance-tested.
